item.title: ‘The game is in danger’: PFA head Maheta Molango on Fifa, Infantino and football’s future
item.description: At a potentially critical juncture for football, the PFA chief executive talks about the organisation, wider fears in the game and why the Folarin Balogun affair was ‘scandalous’ After five years in charge of the Professional Footballers’ Association, what has Maheta Molango learned? “The game is in danger,” the 43-year-old says. “I’ve learned that the game I loved and led me to first play and then advise and then lead a club and today to lead the PFA, is in danger because it is being forgotten.” In 2026, with football ubiquitous on all platforms, with a World Cup that generated $15bn (£11.4m) in revenue, and with attendances across the English pyramid growing year on year, it may seem hard to imagine forgetting about the game. But Molango’s unique perspective as head of the English players’ union observes a different picture; one where the future of the sport is being determined not by what will maintain its popularity, but what will make the most money. Continue reading...

item.title: Danny Kelly obituary
item.description: Ebullient journalist, magazine editor and broadcaster whose passion for music and football shone through all his work Danny Kelly, who has died aged 69, influenced music journalism and sports broadcasting for more than four decades. Humour, enthusiasm and encyclopedic knowledge were the hallmarks of his work as a writer and editor at the New Musical Express (NME) and Q magazine, and throughout his online, TV and audio career, most prominently around his passion for football. In 1997 Kelly helped set up Football 365, one of the earliest football websites, and still one of the most popular in the UK. He hosted radio shows on BBC 5 Live, TalkSport, BT Sport and Times Radio, as well as many podcasts including The View from the Lane, about the team he had supported since childhood, Tottenham Hotspur. Continue reading...

item.title: Pocognoli’s aspiration for how Scotland must play is in danger of becoming unworkable
item.description: The 4-0 debacle against Switzerland has added to the tactical concerns about the head coach’s suitability, just six games into the job The Scottish Football Association can only cling to a lesson from the past when assessing a worrying international window. Steve Clarke was beleaguered during his early games in charge. Successive 4-0 defeats by Belgium and Russia in 2019 left Clarke with the sense he should have stayed in club management. A revival meant Clarke led his country to three out of four tournaments. There are, however, fundamental differences between the story of Clarke and that being delivered by Sébastien Pocognoli. Clarke was a pragmatist, whose decades in coaching suggested he had the wherewithal to revive Scotland. Pocognoli, six games into his tenure, is in danger of lurching into the territory of dreamy ideologue whose aspiration for how Scotland must play is unworkable. item.title: Football Daily | Jürgen Klopp hard-launches his Germany rebuilding project in style
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Barely six weeks ago, Jürgen Klopp’s big home debut in the Germany dugout ended in a deeply frustrating 1-0 Nations League defeat to Greece – but the manager tasked with returning Die Mannschaft to relevance claimed not to care. “I’m completely unbothered,” Klopp trilled unconvincingly. “I’ve lost far more matches than I would have liked, but as long as you draw the right conclusions, a loss is ultimately a piece of information – no different from a win.” It was a quote straight out of the Pierre Sage playbook for unfussed continental coaches – and probably worried a few German FA suits, given Klopp had already threatened to quit at his own unveiling over potential media intrusion and criticism. “If you say tomorrow, ‘he’s [sh!t]’, tell me to my face and I’m out,” Klopp roared to trembling hacks in July . That imagined confrontation now looks unlikely to take place, because his Germany side are suddenly very good indeed. Continue read

item.description: A new film about the historic World Cup quarter-final clash finds new angles for a new generation “Is there anything new to say about it?” Gary Lineker asked the producer Flora Fernandez-Marengo when she first approached him to take part in The Match, a documentary about the 1986 World Cup quarter-final between England and Argentina. item.title: Janine van Wyk: ‘Our rooms were empty … no mattresses, no lightbulbs and not a drop of water’
item.description: In an extract from the former South Africa captain’s book, she details less than ideal Wafcon 2006 preparations I was just a year into my international career when we qualified for my first Wafcon, which was then called the African Women’s Championship (AWC) and was held in Nigeria in 2006. I was extremely excited but very nervous to participate in this tournament, more so when it was announced that we would be in the same group as the hosts, and would play them last in the group. As it turned out, it would be the game that decided who finished top of the group. By then we had beaten Algeria 4-0 and Equatorial Guinea 2-0 and had to travel to Delta State to take on the hosts. I’d heard that Nigeria was the toughest country to travel to and I was about to realise why. It’s become common knowledge that South Africans and Nigerians are massive rivals on the football field but also don’t really get on off it. Continue reading...

item.description: ‘We will not go back on this way of playing,’ says Thomas Tuchel after he delivered response to World Cup critics Thomas Tuchel made defensive substitutions as England protected a lead. He finished with three centre-backs on the pitch. His team could not get out of their half in the final part of the game. So close your eyes and imagine an alternate universe in which James Trafford did not make his stunning double save in stoppage time on Sunday and England had drawn 3-3 with Spain at the Metropolitano Stadium rather than won 3-2 . The reaction would not have been kind because Tuchel has been here before. The head coach wanted to push one particular comparison from the World Cup over the summer. “It was Mexico reloaded,” he said, with a nod towards the 3-2 last-16 win at the Azteca Stadium and it fitted like a glove – down to the detail of Jarell Quansah and red cards. Frank broke his silence at the start of June with a statement released by the League Managers Association. So too the feelings of sadness to see the birds still cooped up in small cages at the nearby bird market. item.title: Record-breaking Andy Robertson is Scotland’s finest captain
item.description: As he passes Kenny Dalglish’s appearance total, it is important to remember that it is the left-back’s journey that sets him apart Andy Robertson may not be Scotland’s greatest player, but he is indisputably their finest captain. It counts as sacrilege, even to generations who have watched Kenny Dalglish only on YouTube, to reputationally place Robertson above the Liverpool hero on the basis of a cap haul that will reach 103 in St Gallen on Monday. Dalglish’s international career ended at 102 and the curious events that meant he missed the 1986 World Cup. There is no requirement to compare a left-back in 2026 to a forward from decades earlier. Dalglish and Robertson are men in different positions in essentially a different sport. Instead, Robertson’s march to the top of the cap pile gives cause to laud his contribution. Continue reading...

item.title: Terry Butcher: ‘I’ve learned to live with the Hand of God goal better’
item.description: The former England centre-back answers your questions on Diego Maradona, Bobby Robson and on staying in strange places “Have you made up all these on your own?” asks Terry Butcher, sitting in a London office in the week he is presented with his England legacy cap. It turns out dozens of Guardian readers want to pick the brains of a much-loved centre-back who was feted en route to a World Cup semi-final and tormented four years previously by the mercurial genius of Diego Maradona. Did Maradona ever admit to the “Hand of God”? Butcher found himself in the post-match doping-control room alongside his nemesis at the Azteca in 1986. “I tapped my head, then my hand, and then he tapped his head,” Butcher says. “He didn’t admit to it because, if he had, I’d have been right across that room.” Continue reading...

item.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership
item.description: Clubs with wealthy proprietors can maintain a loss-making operation but things can be more complex when the supporters carry the can When you walk up from Haydons Road railway station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium. AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter – but that makes running a loss‑making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board, which runs AFC W

item.title: Here Manchester United go again, taking the Two Ronnies route to hiring a new boss | Jonathan Wilson
item.description: Mauricio Pochettino’s arrival feels like yet another appointment that would have been better made a few years ago Magnusson: And your time starts … now! What is paleontology? Smithers: Yes, absolutely correct. Magnusson: What’s the name of the directory that lists members of the peerage? Smithers: A study of old fossils. Magnusson: Correct. Who are Len Murray and Sir Geoffrey Howe? Smithers: Burke’s. Magnusson: Correct. What is the difference between a donkey and an ass? Smithers: One’s a trade union leader, the other’s a member of the Cabinet … One of the Two Ronnies’ most celebrated sketches involves a Mastermind contestant whose specialist subject is answering the previous question. History repeats itself: the first time as comedy, the second time as Manchester United, who seem continually to be answering not the question of who would be the best available manager now, but who might have been the best available manager a few years ago. item.title: Michael Carrick was just the latest fall guy for Manchester United’s dysfunctional hierarchy | Jamie Jackson
item.description: Disastrous decisions and confused appointments have been a constant theme at Old Trafford since Sir Alex Ferguson’s retirement in 2013 For a window into the alarming dysfunction at Manchester United that Michael Carrick failed to manage and caused his sacking , consider the case of Eddie Howe, initially a favourite to succeed the 45-year-old before Mauricio Pochettino’s emergence as the chosen one. The former Newcastle manager had been Jason Wilcox’s choice to take over from Carrick. Howe was also the favoured candidate of Dan Ashworth, Wilcox’s predecessor as United’s director of football, to follow Erik ten Hag after the Dutchman’s sacking in October 2024. Except Wilcox disagreed and Sir Jim Ratcliffe went with Wilcox’s man, Ruben Amorim, and that December Ashworth departed only five months after joining. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘Pregnancy does not mean game over’: meet the footballers challenging the myths | Moving the Goalposts
item.description: Claire Emslie and Emma Kelly are among those taking advantage of new research and guidelines for pregnant players Claire Emslie wasn’t expecting to be able to run at 81% of her max speed at 32 weeks pregnant. Emslie, a Scotland international who also plays as a forward for Angel City FC , documented her journey through pregnancy and football training on social media and is part of a growing number of professional female footballers who are getting pregnant in their athletic prime and approaching motherhood with a fresh mindset. Rather than marking the end of a career (notably, Millie Bright announced her pregnancy in September, months after having retired), pregnancy can mark both a continuation and a renewal. item.title: Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number
item.description: Who is football’s most legendary No 9? Has there ever been a legendary No 28? And why exactly does Mario Balotelli love wearing No 45 so much? Here’s our list and the stories behind it The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure. *** Continue reading...

item.title: Felix Nmecha’s faith is forcing Borussia Dortmund into an uncomfortable debate
item.description: Midfielder’s spectacular strikes rescued a frustrating day, only for celebrations to reignite dialogue that has followed him through his career It was just what they needed at just the right time. For a tricky first half and beyond, Elversberg had been a stone in Borussia Dortmund’s shoe, the promoted side not just keeping the home team at bay but keeping them honest, nourishing ambitions of their own. “The fatigue was clearly visible,” the sporting director, Ole Book, said to Sky after a week which had contained Der Klassiker in Munich and a hard-fought Champions League victory against Betis. “We were a bit too focused on managing the game, which was understandable.” Enter Felix Nmecha. BVB have enjoyed a largely excellent start to the season, are unbeaten and level on points with Bayern Munich at the top; Bayern lead, unsurprisingly, thanks to their superior goal difference. item.title: WSL talking points: Tullis-Joyce takes charge and is Shaw the perfect striker?
item.description: The City forward hit a WSL hat-trick for the ninth time while Eva Olid’s United have found defensive stability Not only did Khadija “Bunny” Shaw score a record-extending ninth WSL hat-trick, she scored a “perfect hat-trick” for the fourth time in the competition, something nobody else has managed more than once. Against West Ham the Jamaica striker opened the scoring with her left foot, headed home her second off the underside of the crossbar and tucked in her third with her right foot late on. It helped her side towards a 5-0 win that opened up a two-point gap at the top of the table and stretched Shaw’s lead in the race to be the top division’s top scorer to a five-goal advantage over her nearest challenger, Océane Hurtré. Can anybody stop her relentless pursuit of another Golden Boot? It would appear not. Tom Garry Match report: Liverpool 1-2 Arsenal Continue reading...

item.title: Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’
item.description: Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. item.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
item.description: Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. Jonathan Wilson Match report: Nottingham Forest 3

item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
